subject: Biotechnology
title: Biotech for Air Quality
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Biotech for Air Quality.

hook.text: Lichens die when air pollution rises — nature's original air quality monitors inspired modern biotech alternatives.

buildup.text: Biofilters use bacterial beds to remove volatile organic compounds from factory exhaust — microbes consume the pollutants.

discovery.text: Biotrickling filters treat hydrogen sulfide from wastewater plants — eliminating the rotten-egg smell with 99% removal efficiency.

twist.text: Living walls with air-purifying plants and root-zone bacteria filter indoor air — but their capacity is debated by scientists.

climax.text: Engineered algae photobioreactors on building facades absorb CO2 and produce oxygen — architecture meets biotechnology.

punchline.text: Breathe cleaner air through biology — biotech purifies what we inhale indoors and out.

quiz.question: How do biofilters clean factory exhaust air?
options: They trap pollutants in chemical solutions for later disposal
Beds of bacteria metabolize volatile organic compounds, breaking them down into harmless substances
They use high-speed fans to dilute pollutants below dangerous levels

details.summary: Biotechnology approaches to air quality include biofilters using microbial communities to remove volatile organic compounds, algae-based CO2 capture systems, engineered plants that metabolize indoor pollutants, and biosensors for real-time air quality monitoring.
details.whyItMatters: Air pollution causes seven million premature deaths annually. Biological air treatment systems can operate sustainably with lower energy requirements than conventional technologies, offering scalable solutions for both industrial emissions and urban
takeaways: Biofilters use microbial communities to metabolize airborne pollutants
Algae bioreactors capture CO2 while producing valuable biomass products
Engineered houseplants can metabolize formaldehyde and other indoor toxins

faq.question: How do biofilters clean polluted air?
faq.answer: Contaminated air passes through beds of organic material colonized by bacteria and fungi. Pollutant molecules dissolve into the biofilm moisture layer where microorganisms metabolize them into harmless compounds.

faq.question: Can plants really improve indoor air quality?
faq.answer: Standard houseplants provide minimal air cleaning at normal densities. However, genetically engineered pothos ivy expressing rabbit CYP2E1 enzyme metabolizes formaldehyde and chloroform effectively. Engineered plants could provide meaningful air purification in enclosed spaces like offices.
